analysis.one_liner: Slashes power plant sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions by 2009.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 100 cosponsors from both parties, was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and sent to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Clean Smokestacks Act would have required the EPA to write rules cutting sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions from large power plants by 75%, mercury by 90%, and carbon dioxide back to 1990 levels by January 1, 2009. It would also have forced power plants that are 30 years old to meet modern pollution standards, closing a grandfathering loophole for the oldest, dirtiest plants. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants, especially in the eastern United States, along with anyone breathing air affected by smog, acid rain, and mercury pollution; the bill also directed EPA to include incentives for renewable energy.

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA to cut power plant sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions by 75% and mercury by 90%, pollutants linked to asthma, heart disease, acid rain, and developmental harm, by January 1, 2009 [S3].
Caps power plant carbon dioxide emissions at 1990 levels, a climate target that a narrow statute had never imposed on the power sector [S3].
Requires power plants 30 years or older to meet the newest performance standards, closing the exemption that let aging plants keep polluting at pre-modern levels [S3].
Directs EPA to prevent localized pollution hotspots and to achieve reductions in both the eastern and western regions, rather than allowing trading to concentrate pollution in one area [S3].
Directs EPA to coordinate with other agencies on energy efficiency and renewable energy to lower the cost of compliance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal- and oil-fired power plants, who would bear retrofit, fuel-switching, or retirement costs, and ratepayers to the extent those costs were passed into electricity prices.

drawbacks.text: Deep, fast emission cuts would impose significant compliance costs on coal-heavy utilities, and some of those costs would flow into household and business electricity bills; the bill itself acknowledges the need to minimize economic costs [S3].

Regions and workers dependent on coal mining and coal-fired generation would bear job losses as plants cut coal use or retired, a burden concentrated in a few states rather than spread nationally [S3].

The 2009 deadlines for all four pollutants were aggressive for an industry with long construction timelines, and critics would argue the bill left too little flexibility, even though it allowed emissions trading for everything except mercury [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains — steep cuts in mercury, smog-forming and acid-rain pollutants, and a carbon cap — would fall on a public that today absorbs those costs as disease and ecosystem damage. The costs, higher power prices in coal-reliant regions and job losses in coal communities, are real and geographically concentrated, and the tight 2009 timeline gave the industry little runway. On balance the bill's benefits to public health outweighed its costs, though a smoother transition schedule would have blunted the strongest objections.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its energy subcommittee, and stayed there until the 108th Congress ended in January 2005 without a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on May 8, 2003 with original cosponsors including both Democrats and Republicans such as Reps. Boehlert, Gilchrest, and LoBiondo [S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on May 8, 2003 [S1].
On May 20, 2003 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained [S5].
The bill attracted 100 cosponsors — 89 Democrats, 10 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but the committee never reported it to the floor before the Congress ended [S4].
No further action appears in the record after the subcommittee referral; the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of aging coal-fired power plants, which avoided mandatory 75% pollution cuts, a 90% mercury reduction, and a requirement to modernize after 30 years. Better-off in the short run were also coal-dependent regions that avoided transition costs, at the price of continued pollution for downwind communities.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was broad and bipartisan — 100 cosponsors including 10 Republicans and 1 Independent — but the committee process, controlled by the Republican majority, produced no action, and the administration favored a rival, less aggressive plan.

industries.note: The bill would force 75% cuts in sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxide, a 90% mercury cut, and modernization of 30-year-old plants — expensive retrofits or retirements. Its interest in killing the bill ran directly against the health interests of people breathing plant emissions.
Deep emission cuts at coal-burning plants reduce coal demand, concentrating job and revenue losses in coal-producing regions.
The bill directs EPA to include incentives for renewable energy and to coordinate on efficiency and clean energy policies to cut costs, expanding markets for cleaner sources.
Ratepayers would face some price increases where utilities passed through compliance costs, offset by health benefits and the bill's cost-minimizing efficiency provisions.
